extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of anthropology, comparative mythology, and ethnology
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical account of how animal-, plant-, and object-worship (totems, fetishes, mythic hybrids, and anthropomorphized celestial bodies) can originate from social naming practices, linguistic limits, and ancestral cults in primitive societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphorical/nickname naming of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons are commonly given nicknames derived from animals, plants, places, or other objects (e.g., 'a bear', 'an old fox', 'carrots', 'Captain Whirlwind').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives many examples among children and adults and across cultures; these nicknames serve as individual identifiers and are the raw material for later tribal or familial names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descent and inheritance of nicknames into family/tribal names
rubrics_metrics.description: Nicknames tend to descend through generations and may become family surnames or tribal names (e.g., 'Jabutí' meaning tortoise becoming the surname).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a nickname-bearing ancestor is notable, his descendants preserve and pride themselves on the name; if the family becomes dominant it can become a tribal designation ('the Wolves'). Examples from Scotland, the Amazon, and other regions are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in the surviving 'other self' of deceased ancestors
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive peoples commonly believe that the other self (spirit) of a deceased ancestor continues to exist and must be propitiated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This belief provides the motive for treating the named object/animal as an entity to propitiate — the ancestor's other self is expected to aid or harm descendants if propitiated or neglected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confounding metaphor with reality (forgetting distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: If tradition fails to preserve the distinction between a metaphorical name and literal reality, descendants will regard an ancestor's nickname as indicating actual descent from the named animal/object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that the forgetting or misinterpretation of metaphor is central: it converts a metaphorical ancestral title into a literal genealogical claim, producing worshipful attitudes toward the animal/object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poverty/indefiniteness of primitive language leading to misinterpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Undeveloped languages lack abstract terms and words for 'name' or for generic categories, making it difficult to convey that a term is a metaphorical name rather than a real referent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting observers of Australians and Tasmanians, the text argues that limited abstraction ('no name for tree', etc.) makes the metaphor→literal confusion inevitable across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of ancestral qualities to the named object (anthropomorphism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an ancestor nicknamed after an object/animal is believed to persist, his perceived attributes and titles are transferred to that object, which is then thought to possess personality and powers like a human.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., a family tradition that an ancestor was 'the Crab' leads to conceiving the crab as having an inner power or personality; descriptive epithets of a warrior (swift one, destroyer) can be ascribed to a sun or moon once identified with him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation of fetishism as a secondary product
rubrics_metrics.description: Fetichism (belief that objects have personal powers/selves) is produced secondarily from the process of nickname inheritance and misinterpretation, rather than being the primary psychological starting point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues against theories that posit primordial fetishistic thought, showing instead how numerous imaginary personalities for surrounding objects naturally arise from inherited names and beliefs about ancestor-spirits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for anthropomorphic biographies of celestial/terrestrial agents
rubrics_metrics.description: Human biographies attached to celestial or terrestrial objects (sun, moon, rivers) arise because distinguished persons metaphorically named after them became identified with those objects by later tradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This account explains why myths assign specific genealogies, births, loves, and adventures to non-human agents — these are human traditions transferred to the object after misidentification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of hybrid/compound monsters via mixed ancestral nicknames
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories and worship of compound monsters (half-man half-beast, hybrid gods) result when traditions preserve ancestry from individuals nicknamed after different animals/objects, producing genealogies combining attributes and hence hybrids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by examples: a warrior nicknamed 'the Greyhound' and a wife from another animal-nicknamed tribe can yield a tradition of a race descended from a red greyhound and a queen, producing hybrid idols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation for ascription of sex/gender to natural objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Masculine or feminine characters assigned to sky, earth, dawn, etc., follow from ancestral nicknames: if the person nicknamed after an object was male or female, the object later acquires that gender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an account for Max Müller’s observation about gendered nouns in ancient languages: the sex-character of words can be rooted in human ancestors' sexes reflected in nicknames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of names for the same celestial/terrestrial object
rubrics_metrics.description: A single object (e.g., the sun) may have several proper names (Apollo, Helios, Endymion) because different tribes independently used the same metaphorical object-name for different individuals whose traditions later merged with that object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than treating such contradictions as failures of tradition, they are evidence that multiple human individuals provided metaphorical names for the same object in different locales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuation of nicknaming causing double sets of distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after proper names emerge, the practice of nicknaming continues for each new generation, producing both ancestral (tribal) names and individual epithets simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This overlapping of name-systems makes it likely that new nicknames will be misinterpreted as actual names during transitional linguistic stages, fostering mythic identifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive/analytic criterion: misinterpretation is inevitable given linguistic and social conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the combined conditions of nickname practice, descent of names, belief in ancestral spirits, and impoverished abstract language, the author claims misinterpretation (and thus animal-worship, fetichism, hybrid myths, anthropomorphic celestial narratives) is not merely possible but certain to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the capstone claim tying the listed elements together; the text repeatedly argues from ethnographic examples that the sequence produces the observed variety of myths and cults.
